question: How wide are the court lines, and what's the call when a shuttle lands on a line?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) the width of the court lines — answered by laws-1.1 (1): 'The court shall be a rectangle marked out with lines 40 mm wide as shown in Diagram A.' (2) the call when a shuttle lands on a line — answered by laws-1.3 (1): 'All the lines shall form part of the area which they define' (so a shuttle on a line is in), and laws-13.3.1 (1)-(2): a fault only if the shuttle 'lands outside the boundaries of the court (i.e. not on or within the boundary lines)'. The umpire's call rule itto-5.8.3.1 (1) ('Out' when the shuttle lands outside the line) also bears directly on the call, so it is included for part 2. No para-badminton rules are needed since the question is about standard play.
answer.answer: The court is a rectangle marked out with lines 40 mm wide [1]. A shuttle that lands on a line is in, because all the lines form part of the area which they define [2], and a shuttle is only out when it lands outside the boundaries of the court, that is, not on or within the boundary lines [3][4]. So the call is not "Out", since "Out" is called only when the shuttle lands outside the line [5]. When the shuttle lands in, the Line Judge says nothing but points to the line with the right hand while looking towards the Umpire [6].

question: How do we check whether a shuttle has the right speed?

answer.reasoning: The question asks how to check whether a shuttle has the right speed. I searched the rule books and found Law 3 'Testing a shuttle for speed': Law 3.1 (laws-3.1) states how the shuttle must be hit in the test — a full underhand stroke contacting the shuttle over the back boundary line, hit at an upward angle parallel to the side lines (sentences 1 and 2). Law 3.2 (laws-3.2) states the criterion for correct speed — the shuttle lands not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line (sentence 1, referencing Diagram B). The Instructions to Technical Officials add the procedure around the test: itto-3.5.4.1 (tested by an active player, preferably male, or a qualified person approved by the Referee), itto-3.5.4.2 (all available speeds tested from both ends of the court), and itto-3.5.4.4 (assess the result considering strength of shot, trajectory, and whether hit from over the back line). Related but not directly answering: itto-3.5.4 (Referee oversees testing before the first day's play) and itto-3.6.3 (Referee considers during play whether the selected speed still appears correct).
answer.answer: The Referee shall oversee the testing of shuttles prior to the start of the first day's play [7], and the shuttles should be tested by an active player in the tournament, preferably a male player, or a qualified person approved by the Referee [4], with all available speeds tested from both ends of the court [5]. To test a shuttle, the player shall use a full underhand stroke which makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line [1], hitting it at an upward angle and in a direction parallel to the side lines [2]. Law 4.3.2(1) (laws-4.3.2, sentence 1) adds the companion prohibition on any device that materially changes the racket's shape, which completes what is and is not allowed. No Alternative Laws variant alters Law 4, and no para-badminton rule is relevant to this standard-play question.

question: When is my racket allowed to cross over the net?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: when a player's racket is allowed to cross over the net. The Laws answer it in Law 13.4.2(1): invading the opponent's court over the net with racket or person is a fault, except that the striker may follow the shuttle over the net with the racket in the course of a stroke after the initial point of contact with the shuttle is on the striker's side of the net. That single numbered sentence contains both the prohibition and the exception, so it answers the part. Related but non-answering sentences: Law 13.4.4(2) (even when the shuttle is followed over the net, preventing an opponent from making a legal stroke is a fault), Law 13.4.1(1) (touching the net with racket is a fault), and ITTO 5.9.1.1(1) (throwing a racket into the opponent's court is faulted under Law 13.4.2). No Alternative Laws clause alters 13.4.2 (the Alternative Laws cover scoring and service only), and no para rule is needed since the question is about standard play.
answer.answer: Your racket is allowed to cross over the net only when you are the striker following the shuttle over the net with the racket in the course of a stroke, and only after the initial point of contact with the shuttle is on your side of the net [1]. question: How far from the court lines should the line judges sit?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing: the distance from the court lines at which line judges should sit. ITTO Clause 8.9 answers it directly: sentence (1) recommends, where practical, that Line Judges' positions be 2.5 to 3.5 metres from the court boundaries (with the condition 'where practical' attached, so the sentence with the condition is picked), and sentence (2) completes that same sentence's example about protection from outside influence. ITTO 8.1 (sitting on chairs directly looking down their designated lines) bears on line judge positioning but does not answer the distance, so it goes in related_sentences.

question: What's the minimum rest a player gets between two matches?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: the minimum rest a player is entitled to between two matches. ITTO clause 3.5.17.4 answers it directly: sentence (1) gives the standard minimum of a 60-minute interval between matches, reducible by the Referee in exceptional circumstances to no less than 30 minutes; sentence (2) gives a 30-minute minimum for junior, junior team, Para badminton tournaments and qualifying rounds. Sentence (3) of the same clause (Referee should try to provide a longer interval) and ITTO 3.5.17.5 (avoid disproportionate rest times between opponents) bear on the topic without stating the minimum, so they go in related_sentences. Law 16.2 intervals concern rest between games within a match, not between matches, so they do not answer this part.
answer.answer: A player is entitled to a minimum 60-minute interval between two matches, and in exceptional circumstances the Referee can reduce the interval to no less than 30 minutes [1]. In Junior tournaments, Junior team tournaments, Para badminton tournaments, and qualifying rounds of other tournaments, with the rule in force 2025-04-26, the player is entitled to a minimum 30-minute interval between two matches [2]. The Referee should try to provide a longer interval between any two matches of a given player, and in particular between a player's matches in the same event [3]. Opposing sides in a match should not have disproportionately different rest times since their previous round matches in that event [4].

question: We forgot to switch ends at 11 in the third game and only noticed at 14-12. What now?

answer.reasoning: The question has three parts: (1) when ends must be changed in the third game — answered by Laws of Badminton 8.1.3(1) ('in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches'), with the Alternative Laws best-of-3-games-21 version 8.1.3(1) stating the same without the handicap exception; (2) what to do when the change was missed and is only noticed later (at 14-12) — answered by Law 8.2(1): change ends as soon as the mistake is discovered and when the shuttle is not in play; (3) what happens to the points already played — answered by Law 8.2(2): the existing score shall stand. The ITTO 5.6.10(1) umpire call at 11 in the third game bears on the question without answering a part, so it goes in related_sentences.
answer.answer: Change ends now, as soon as the mistake is discovered and when the shuttle is not in play [3]. In the third game, players must change ends when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches [1]. question: What should an umpire do when they're not sure whether a fault happened?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing: what an umpire should do when unsure whether a fault occurred. ITTO Clause 6.8 (1) answers this directly: if a doubt arises as to whether an infringement of the Laws has occurred, the umpire must not call a 'fault' and must allow the game to proceed. ITTO Clause 2.5 (2) bears on the question without answering it: when no decision can be made (e.g., an official is unsighted), a 'let' is called unless IRS is in use, so it goes in related_sentences.

question: What does a black card mean, and who decides to give it?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what a black card means, and (2) who decides to give it. The Laws of Badminton (Law 16.7.2, sentence 1) state that on faulting a side the umpire reports to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match. The Instructions to Technical Officials (5.17.5) give the black card procedure: sentence (1) says when the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair, a black card is given to the Umpire; sentences (3) and (4) say the Umpire announces the player(s) 'disqualified for misconduct' while raising the black card. So the black card means disqualification for misconduct, and the Referee is the one who decides (the Umpire displays it). Related: ITTO 3.6.2.2 (1) notes a disqualified player is disqualified from all events of the tournament, and Law 13.5 (1) makes flagrant/repeated/persistent offences under Law 16 a fault — these bear on the question without answering either part directly.
answer.answer: A black card signals that the offending player or pair is disqualified for misconduct, and the Referee decides to give it [1][4]. When the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair, a black card is given to the Umpire [1]. The Umpire then calls "Come here" to the offending player or pair, announces "[name of player(s)], disqualified for misconduct" followed by a specific explanation of the misconduct, and at the same time raises the right hand holding the black card above the Umpire's head [2][3]. On faulting a side, the umpire reports the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match [4]. Should the Referee decide to disqualify a player, this player is disqualified from all events of the tournament and, in Team Tournaments, from all future matches of the Team Tournament [5].

question: My string broke during a rally. What am I allowed to do about my racket?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing in two aspects: (1) what a player may do about the racket when a string breaks during a rally, and (2) under what conditions (leaving the court, delaying play). Part 1 is answered directly by ITTO 5.10.1 sentence (2): 'A change of a racket at courtside during a rally is permitted.' Part 2 is answered by ITTO 5.10.1 sentence (1) and Law 16.5.2 sentence (1): a player may not leave the court during a match without the umpire's permission, causing delay, except during Law 16.2 intervals. The Laws list no let or fault for a broken string specifically; the nearest rule is Law 14.2.7 (let for 'any unforeseen or accidental situation'), which goes in related_sentences, along with ITTO 5.11.1 sentence (2) on preventing unnecessary testing of replacement rackets between rallies.
answer.answer: If a string breaks during a rally, you are permitted to change your racket at courtside during that rally [1]. To do so you must not leave the court during the match without the umpire's permission or cause delay to play, except during the intervals described in Law 16.2 [2][3]. If the break is an unforeseen or accidental situation, it shall be a let [4]. The umpire will prevent any unnecessary walk around the court between rallies and any testing of a replacement racket on court, and will apply Law 16.7 if necessary [5].

question: I play wheelchair badminton. What do the rules allow if I need to leave the court to catheterise?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing: what the rules allow a wheelchair badminton player who needs to leave the court to catheterise. The direct answer is the Para Badminton exception in Law 16.5.3: sentence (1) allows one additional interval during a match to leave the court to catheterise, and sentence (2) requires the player to be accompanied by any BWF appointed Technical Official. The general rule in Law 16.5.2 (no player leaves the court during a match without the umpire's permission, except during Law 16.2 intervals) is the rule this para exception modifies, so it goes in related_sentences along with the ITTO umpire instruction that mirrors it. No other part of the question lacks an answer.
answer.answer: In Wheelchair Badminton, the Para Badminton rule in force 2025-04-26 allows you to leave the court for one additional interval during a match in order to catheterise [1]. You shall be accompanied by any BWF appointed Technical Official [2]. The general rule is that no player shall leave the court during a match without the umpire's permission [3], and the umpire shall ensure that players do not leave without permission except during the intervals, or that they do not delay play [4].

question: How many seconds does the server have to serve once the receiver is ready?

Law 9.4(1) covers the related rule that the server shall not serve before the receiver is ready. Because the assumed fixed number contradicts the sources, these sentences give the sources' version and answer the part. Related sentences: Law 9.1.2(1) (delay after the backward movement of the racket head is undue delay), Law 14.2.1(1) (let if the server serves before the receiver is ready), and Law 16.4.2(1) (the umpire is the sole judge of any delay in play) bear on the question without stating a number of seconds.
